closed_this_pass.what: BypassSink as a real UDP NAT path for verdict Bypass (SPEC §6.10, §6.8)
closed_this_pass.decision_log: implementation-notes.md, section 'Этап 8 — BypassSink: настоящий NAT-путь для bypass (§6.10, §6.8)'

changed_files.what: ParseUDP4(pkt []byte) (src, dst netip.AddrPort, payload []byte, ok bool) — standalone IPv4/UDP parse, deliberately not sharing code with netstack.parse so internal/bypass does not import internal/netstack.

New package. NAT — full-cone UDP NAT keyed only by client src addr:port (never dst, unlike netstack's natTable — full-cone is why mDNS replies from a unicast responder address still reach the client). Sockets opened via (&net.ListenConfig{Control: cfg.Control}).ListenPacket(ctx, "udp4", ":0") so every socket is bound to the physical interface (§6.8) the same way Xray/health-probe/subscription sockets already are. Send(pkt) returns ErrDisabled when policy.BypassSink is off, ErrUnsupported when the packet is not IPv4/UDP. Idle sweep is lazy (on Send and on Stats()), no background ticker.

Stack.Deliver(pkt []byte) — the reply path back into the TUN device, through the same s.write single-writer that natTable/tcpStack already use. netstack.go:259 handle() calls s.cfg.Bypass.Send(pkt) for verdict Bypass and discards the error (same silent-drop shape as before when Bypass is nil or disabled).

Config.BypassControl bypass.ControlFunc (nil in tests that don't want a real sink; Config.Bypass stays as the older test substitution point). Agent.bypassNAT *bypass.NAT, built in Up() when Config.Bypass is nil and BypassControl is set, torn down symmetrically in Down() and watchService(), same lifetime as a.stack. Agent.deliverBypass(pkt []byte) — same deferred-closure-over-a.stack trick already used by InterruptConnections and Prober.

run() takes a third function parameter bypassControl bypass.ControlFunc, symmetric to the existing dialDirect parameter; main() passes physical.Control (the same *outbound.Selector already used for Interface()/DialDirect).

New policy BypassSink (bypass_sink). It gates the real sink's construction/use inside internal/bypass (ErrDisabled from NAT.Send), not the call site in netstack.handle — turning off the call site would also redden TestT17MDNSGoesToLocalNetwork, which must stay green (verdict-only, unaffected by delivery).

new_tests.note: Real UDP sockets on loopback, no transport mocks. The first two are the negcheck guards for policy bypass_sink.

Agent-level, over a loopback listener, on a fake device (no netns/privileges) — proves the wiring (Up builds the sink, packet round-trips through netstack.Deliver) without proving physical-interface binding, which is L3's job. Fix round 1 (post-review): the test must build its Agent with NewXray set to the package's fake xray factory, matching every other test in internal/agent — the first version accidentally used a real xray-core instance and only worked by the accident of an empty node list.

linux-only, real netns + veth pair, registered in SPEC.md §8.4 as T31. Forces mDNS (224.0.0.251:5353) into the TUN with an ip rule at priority 20000 (below hopd's own prioExclusions=31000, so it doesn't fight hopd's rules) — the §6.10 case where the ordinary exclusion rule didn't hold. A responder added to internal/l3/routecache_test.go's peerMain joins the mDNS group and echoes both the payload and the source address it observed. Three separate assertions: the peer received the request; the source address it saw is the physical interface's address (10.9.9.1, veth0), not the tunnel client's (10.255.0.1) — this positive+negative pair is what catches a transparent-forward regression; the client received the reply from the responder's address.

measurements: ip rule add to 224.0.0.251/32 lookup <table> priority N with N < prioExclusions(31000) pulls exactly that multicast group into the tunnel table without touching hopd's own rules (31000/31500/32000) or other multicast (verified against SSDP, 239.255.255.250 unaffected). Verified with TX packet counters on a dummy interface before/after sendto, not just `ip route get` (route cache can be mistaken for the actual routing decision).

Sending to a multicast address does not require IGMP group membership (that's only needed to receive); receiving on the peer side does require IP_ADD_MEMBERSHIP (net.ListenMulticastUDP) — without it the kernel drops the inbound datagram at the IP layer even though the frame physically arrived on veth1. Standard host IGMP membership behavior, not veth-specific.

net.ListenPacket("udp4", ...) on Linux (go1.26.3) returns a *net.UDPConn whose ReadFrom yields a *net.UDPAddr (not a string) — bypass.socket's direct type assertion a.(*net.UDPAddr) is sufficient; the netip.ParseAddrPort(a.String()) fallback that netstack.addrPort carries wasn't needed for sockets opened this way. Recorded in implementation-notes.md, not just the task report.
deviations: Only UDP. bypass.NAT.Send returns ErrUnsupported for anything that isn't IPv4/UDP; TCP to a LAN address (RFC1918/loopback/link-local, verdict Bypass via isBypass, internal/netstack/verdict.go:119) is still silently dropped by netstack.handle, exactly as before this pass. Reason: §6.10's exceptions are for service discovery, which is entirely UDP; §6.8 names UDP full-cone (§5.3) as bypass's own return path; an honest TCP path would need stream termination inside gvisor, and that relay would land in the §5.5 interrupt registry, whose 'tear the connection down when the node dies' semantics are wrong for traffic that never went through a node. This was a decision taken before task 1 started (constraints.md), not discovered during implementation — queued as future work, not an open question.

DHCP through a NAT socket cannot be faithful. The client's source port 68 gets rewritten to an ephemeral port (bypass.NAT keys only on source address via the socket, not on preserving the source port), and binding a port below 1024 is unavailable to an unprivileged agent. §6.10 lists DHCP among the exceptions routed to bypass, but a real DHCP exchange through this NAT path will not work correctly. In practice this rarely bites: the machine's own DHCP lease is handled by the OS before hop up runs, outside netstack's verdicts entirely. What remains genuinely open is DHCP-relay or any other transit traffic on port 67/68 originating from inside the tunnel.

next_task.why_first: First item of the queue that was already deferred behind BypassSink; now that BypassSink delivers packets for real, a fixed hardcoded list is the next thing standing between the spec's routing description and what the config can actually express.
current_state: internal/netstack/verdict.go:119, isBypass(f flow) bool — hardcoded logic: RFC1918/loopback/link-local ranges plus §5.6's always-allowed exceptions (DHCP, NTP), plus mDNS (224.0.0.251:5353, [ff02::fb]:5353) and SSDP for service discovery (§6.10). None of this is configurable at runtime; the address set isn't read from any config struct.

internal/netstack/verdict.go:76, classify(f flow, healthy bool) Verdict — calls isBypass(f) directly; verdict order (bypass vs DNS hijack) is already a policy (VerdictOrder), but the bypass membership test itself is not.
BypassSink (this pass) delivers whatever verdict Bypass hands it — it has no opinion on which flows get that verdict. Wiring the actual list is entirely verdict.go's concern.
next_task.goal: Whatever set of addresses/prefixes/ports isBypass currently hardcodes should instead be derived from configuration, so a user (or a future default profile) can extend or narrow what goes to the physical interface instead of the tunnel, without a code change. The always-on §5.6 exceptions (loopback, RFC1918, link-local, DHCP, NTP) are not what needs to become configurable — SPEC.md doesn't say they should be; what's hardcoded and plausibly meant to be a list is the service-discovery bypass set (mDNS/SSDP) and the general shape of 'other bypass/block lists' from the plan and HANDOFF's prior queue entry.
reuse: internal/policy already has the pattern for a guarded on/off flag (BypassSink, this pass) — a configurable list needs a different shape (a value, not a bool), so check whether internal/policy or another package already has a precedent for a configurable value (not just flag) before inventing one.
internal/bypass and the Deliver/Config.Bypass wiring from this pass are unaffected by this task — verdict.go decides membership before bypass.NAT ever sees a packet.

notes.realtimelint: does not accept ./... as an argument — pass literally `.`
notes.l3_how_to_run: Build once, run under an unprivileged user namespace: `go test -c -o /tmp/l3.test ./internal/l3` then `HOP_L3=1 unshare -Urn /tmp/l3.test` (add `-test.v -test.run '<pattern>'` to scope it). This works without root — unshare -Urn grants CAP_NET_ADMIN inside the fresh netns. Building the test binary once and reusing it across repeated unshare invocations is much faster than `go test` per run when iterating.
